paragraphs: To judge accurately the proper extent of the federal judiciary, it will be necessary first to consider what its proper objects are.

It seems hardly open to dispute that the judicial authority of the Union ought to extend to these several kinds of cases: 1st, all those that arise out of the laws of the United States, passed in accordance with their just and constitutional powers of legislation; 2d, all those that concern the execution of the provisions expressly contained in the articles of Union; 3d, all those in which the United States are a party; 4th, all those that involve the PEACE of the CONFEDERACY, whether they concern the dealings between the United States and foreign nations or those between the States themselves; 5th, all those that originate on the high seas and fall under admiralty or maritime jurisdiction; and lastly, all those in which the State courts cannot be supposed to be impartial and unbiased.

The first point rests on this obvious consideration: there ought always to be a constitutional method of giving effect to constitutional provisions. What, for instance, would restrictions on the authority of the State legislatures be worth without some constitutional means of enforcing them? Under the plan of the Convention the States are forbidden to do a variety of things, some of which are incompatible with the interests of the Union and others with the principles of good government. Imposing duties on imported articles and issuing paper money are examples of each kind. No sensible man will believe that such prohibitions would be scrupulously respected unless the government had some effective power to restrain or correct violations of them. This power must be either a direct negative on the State laws, or an authority in the federal courts to overrule those that were in manifest contravention of the articles of Union. I can imagine no third course. The Convention appears to have thought the latter preferable to the former, and, I presume, the latter will be more agreeable to the States.

As to the second point, no argument or comment can make it clearer than it is in itself. If there are such things as political axioms, the principle that the judicial power of a government should be coextensive with its legislative may be ranked among them. The mere need for uniformity in interpreting the national laws settles the question. Thirteen independent courts of final jurisdiction over the same causes, arising upon the same laws, would be a hydra in government, from which nothing but contradiction and confusion can come.

Still less need be said about the third point. Controversies between the nation and its members or citizens can properly be referred only to the national courts. Any other plan would be contrary to reason, to precedent and to decorum.

The fourth point rests on this plain proposition: the peace of the WHOLE ought not to be left at the disposal of a PART. The Union will undoubtedly be answerable to foreign powers for the conduct of its members. And responsibility for an injury ought always to come with the ability to prevent it. The denial or perversion of justice by the sentences of courts, like any other denial or perversion of it, is rightly classed among the just causes of war. It follows that the federal judiciary ought to have jurisdiction over all cases in which the citizens of other countries are concerned. This is no less essential to preserving the public faith than to securing the public tranquillity. A distinction may perhaps be imagined between cases arising under treaties and the laws of nations and those that rest merely on municipal law. The former kind may be thought proper for federal jurisdiction, the latter for that of the States. But it is at least doubtful whether an unjust sentence against a foreigner, in a controversy that was wholly a matter of the lex loci, would not, if left unredressed, be an aggression against his sovereign, as well as a violation of the stipulations of a treaty or of the general law of nations. And there would be a still greater objection to the distinction, in the immense difficulty, if not impossibility, of telling in practice the cases of one kind from those of the other. So large a proportion of the cases in which foreigners are parties involve national questions that it is by far the safest and most expedient course to refer all of them to the national courts.

The power of deciding causes between two States, between one State and the citizens of another, and between the citizens of different States is perhaps no less essential to the peace of the Union than the power just examined. History gives us a horrid picture of the dissensions and private wars that distracted and desolated Germany before Maximilian, toward the close of the fifteenth century, established the Imperial Chamber. It tells us at the same time of the vast influence of that institution in calming the disorders and establishing the tranquillity of the empire. This was a court invested with authority to decide finally all differences among the members of the Germanic body.

A method of ending territorial disputes between the States, under the authority of the federal head, was not overlooked even in the imperfect system by which they have been held together until now. But there are many other sources, besides conflicting claims of boundary, from which quarrels and animosities may arise among the members of the Union. We have witnessed some of these in our past experience. It will readily be guessed that I allude to the fraudulent laws passed in too many of the States. And though the proposed Constitution establishes particular safeguards against a repetition of the instances that have appeared before, it is reasonable to fear that the spirit that produced them will take new shapes, which could not be foreseen or specifically provided against. Whatever practices tend to disturb the harmony between the States are proper objects of federal superintendence and control.

It may be considered the basis of the Union that "the citizens of each State shall be entitled to all the privileges and immunities of citizens of the several States." And if it is a sound principle that every government ought to have the means of executing its own provisions by its own authority, it follows that, in order to maintain inviolably the equality of privileges and immunities to which the citizens of the Union will be entitled, the national judiciary ought to preside in all cases in which one State or its citizens are opposed to another State or its citizens. To secure the full effect of so fundamental a provision against all evasion and subterfuge, its interpretation must be committed to that court which, having no local attachments, is likely to be impartial between the different States and their citizens, and which, owing its official existence to the Union, will never be likely to feel any bias unfavorable to the principles on which the Union is founded.

The fifth point will call for little comment. The most bigoted worshipers of State authority have not so far shown any disposition to deny the national judiciary jurisdiction over maritime causes. These so generally depend on the laws of nations, and so commonly affect the rights of foreigners, that they fall within the considerations that concern the public peace. The most important of them are, under the present Confederation, submitted to federal jurisdiction.

That the national courts should act where the State courts cannot be presumed impartial is self-evident. No one should be judge in his own cause, or in any cause in which he has the slightest interest or bias. This principle weighs heavily in making the federal courts the proper courts for controversies between different States and their citizens. It should apply as well to some cases between citizens of one State. Claims to land under grants from different States, resting on opposing claims about boundaries, are of this kind. The courts of neither granting State could be expected to be unbiased. The laws may even have prejudged the question and bound the courts to rule for the grants of their own State. And even where that had not been done, the judges, being men, would naturally lean strongly toward the claims of their own government.

Having set out and discussed the principles that should shape the federal judiciary, we will now use them to test the particular powers that, under the plan of the Convention, make it up. It is to comprehend "all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution, the laws of the United States, and treaties made, or which shall be made, under their authority; to all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls; to all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction; to controversies to which the United States shall be a party; to controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States; between citizens of the same State claiming lands and grants of different States; and between a State or the citizens thereof and foreign states, citizens, and subjects." This is the whole body of the Union's judicial authority. Let us now go through it item by item. It is, then, to extend:

First. To all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution and the laws of the United States. This corresponds with the first two classes of causes that I listed as proper for the jurisdiction of the United States. It has been asked what is meant by "cases arising under the Constitution," as distinguished from those "arising under the laws of the United States." The difference has already been explained. All the restrictions on the authority of the State legislatures furnish examples of it. The States are not, for instance, to issue paper money; but that prohibition comes from the Constitution and will have no connection with any law of the United States. Should paper money be issued notwithstanding, the controversies about it would be cases arising under the Constitution and not under the laws of the United States, in the ordinary meaning of those terms. This may serve as a sample of the whole.

It has also been asked why the word "equity" is needed. What equitable causes can grow out of the Constitution and laws of the United States? Hardly any lawsuit between individuals fails to involve some element of fraud, accident, trust or hardship that would make it a matter for equitable rather than legal jurisdiction, as the distinction is known and established in several of the States. For instance, it is the special province of a court of equity to give relief against what are called hard bargains. These are contracts in which there may have been no direct fraud or deceit sufficient to void them in a court of law, yet one party took some undue and unconscionable advantage of the other's needs or misfortunes, which a court of equity will not tolerate. In such cases, where foreigners were involved on either side, the federal courts could not do justice without equitable as well as legal jurisdiction. Agreements to convey lands claimed under grants from different States may supply another example of why the federal courts need equitable jurisdiction. This argument may be less obvious in those States where the formal and technical distinction between LAW and EQUITY is not kept up, as it is in this State, where every day's practice shows it.
The judicial authority of the Union is to extend:

Second. Treaties made, or to be made, under the authority of the United States, and all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls. These fall under the fourth class of cases I listed, because of their evident link to preserving the national peace.
Third. To cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction. Together these form the fifth of the classes of causes I listed as proper for the jurisdiction of the national courts.
Fourth. To controversies to which the United States shall be a party. These make up the third of those classes.

Fifth. Controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States. These fall under the fourth of those classes and, to some degree, share the nature of the last.

Sixth. Cases between citizens of the same State claiming lands under grants from different States. These come within the last class, and they are the only instances in which the proposed Constitution directly provides for jurisdiction over disputes between citizens of one State.

Seventh. To cases between a State or its citizens and foreign states, citizens or subjects. These have already been explained as belonging to the fourth of the classes I listed, and have been shown to be, in a special way, proper subjects for the national judiciary.

This review of the particular powers of the federal judiciary, as marked out in the Constitution, shows that they all conform to the principles that ought to have governed the structure of that department, and that were necessary to the perfection of the system. If some particular problems should appear to be connected with including any of them in the plan, we should remember that the national legislature will have ample authority to make such exceptions, and to prescribe such regulations, as are calculated to prevent or remove those problems. A well-informed mind can never regard the possibility of particular harms as a solid objection to a general principle that is meant to avoid general harms and to obtain general advantages.
